name: Changsha dialect
confidence_why: Changsha's six lexical tones are uncontested, and the initial-strong disyllabic pattern measured by Guo and Chen 2022 is confirmed rather than challenged by Zhang, Gong and Guo 2026, who add a final-strong pattern in certain compound types and in proper names and stop short of calling the prominence stress, so the record rests on one research group's two instrumental studies with no contradiction.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Changsha Xiang is a six-tone language; in ordinary disyllabic (prosodic) words the first syllable is metrically strong (trochaic / left-dominant): it is longer (mean ratio 1.53:1) and keeps its citation tone, while the second syllable is shortened and its tone levelled to a sandhi (near-neutral) tone. A right-dominant (final-strong) pattern with sandhi on the first syllable occurs in a restricted set of structures (per Lin 2011 and Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026: subject-predicate, verb-object, verb-resultative phrases and proper names).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Changsha; Zhong 2007 (abstract) proposes a multi-level metrical structure (syllable, foot, colon, prosodic word) in which some stress-level distinctions are not phonetically realised.
new_statements.exceptions: Right-dominant (final-prominent) structures limited to 'a few grammatical categories' (Guo & Chen); per Lin 2011 abstract and Zhang et al. 2026 slides these are subject-predicate, verb-object, verb-result constructions and proper names; trisyllabic sandhi directionality is not morphosyntactically governed (Lin 2011). Young speakers merge T13/T24 (Zhang et al.).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns disyllabic prosodic words (lexical compounds) produced in a carrier sentence; prominence is diagnosed via tone-sandhi dominance, duration and contour preservation rather than via an independent stress phoneme. Phrase-level prominence (V-O etc.) patterns differently (right-dominant).
new_statements.identity_note: All stress statements found concern the Changsha (長沙) city dialect, the standard representative of New Xiang (Glottolog xian1251 > Chang-Yi subgroup, Changsha; ISO hsn). Peng 2022 (also examined) describes Cenchuan in Pingjiang county, a Gan/Xiang transitional variety, and says nothing about word stress beyond listing qingsheng (toneless) particles/suffixes. Guo & Chen 2022 explicitly restrict their Changsha claim to left-dominant disyllabic prosodic words and note that a right-dominant pattern exists for a few grammatical structures (verb-object, subject-predicate, verb-resultative, proper names per Lin 2011 / Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Six-tone language; word-level prominence ('dominance') is signalled through tone sandhi and duration rather than a fixed stress position. In left-dominant disyllables the first syllable is dominant and the second is neutralised to one of four short level tones; in right-dominant disyllables the final syllable is dominant and the initial syllable is only reduced (undershoot), not neutralised. The same authors' 2026 Lancaster slides on the same study (held by the project) add: dominance is structure-dependent after Lin 2011 (left-in the dominant set coordinative and modifier-head compounds, i.e. most common nouns; right-in the dominant set subject-predicate, verb-result and verb-object structures and always in person/place names); 'Dominant syllables are longer than non-dominant syllables (~ 100ms), consistent with the metrical prominence of the dominant syllables'; but 'More research, both phonetic and phonological, is needed to establish stress in Changsha Xiang.' So: a possible, not yet established, stress system riding on tone sandhi.
new_statements.exceptions: Per the slides: proper nouns (person and place names) are always final-dominant regardless of syllable count (文明 'civilization' left-dominant vs. 文明 the game title right-dominant; 红旗 'red flag' vs. 洪齐 'Hong Qi'); the string 炒饭 is right-dominant as V-Obj 'to stir-fry rice' but left-dominant as the noun 'fried rice'; 'Things are more complicated beyond disyllables'; earlier descriptions may have conflated word- and phrase-level tonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe urban Changsha city Xiang (Zhang et al.: 16 speakers who grew up in and live in Changsha and still distinguish T13 and T24; young city speakers are merging T13/T24 and losing the fall of T42).

new_statements.quote: [SSRN abstract, v2 4702575] Two experiments were conducted to investigate disyllabic words with initial and final stress. The F0 contour and duration analyses showed that the variability in tonal production could be grasped by the interaction of lexical tones and three different levels of stress: primary stress, secondary stress, and no stress. The so-called word-initial unstressed syllables are likelier to be “secondarily stressed” rather than “unstressed”. The six tones retained their underlying targets in both the primary-stressed and secondary-stressed syllables. In the word-final unstressed syllables, the tones merged into four level tones.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (classification tonal; Guo & Chen 2022: Changsha = left-dominant strong-weak disyllables with sigma2 reduced to level tones, right-dominant pattern limited to some grammatical categories) and adds detail: the exact neutralisation mapping to four level tones, the list of structures taking each pattern, the left/right asymmetry (neutralisation only word-finally; initial non-dominant syllables merely undershoot), a ~100 ms / 1.4x duration advantage for dominant syllables, and an explicit hedge that word stress in Changsha Xiang is not yet established. No contradiction in placement or type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Changsha Xiang has six lexical tones (21, 13, 24, 34, 42, 45). Disyllabic sequences are either left-dominant (common nouns; coordinative and modifier-head structures: sigma1 keeps its full tone, sigma2 is paradigmatically neutralised to one of four short level tones, 21->2, 13/34->3, 42/24->4, 45->5) or right-dominant (disyllabic person names; subject-predicate, verb-resultative, verb-object structures: sigma2 keeps its full tone, sigma1 shows phonetic F0 undershoot without neutralisation). Acoustically (16 speakers) dominant syllables are ~100 ms longer (359 vs 258 ms, ~1.4x), have larger F0 excursions and resist tonal coarticulation; the authors read dominance as word-level metrical prominence analogous to stress (sandhi rules written with [+stress] context) but state that a stress system in Changsha Xiang is not yet firmly established and that utterance-final elicitation confounds lexical with phrasal prominence for the right-dominant type.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the article uses a binary dominant/non-dominant contrast (the preprint's three-level scale with secondary stress does not appear).
new_statements.exceptions: Dominance is structure- and category-dependent rather than fixed: modifier-head nouns and coordinatives left-dominant; person names, subject-predicate, verb-resultative and verb-object right-dominant (Table 3 after Lin 2011; minimal pairs common noun vs homophonous person name, e.g. 'red flag' vs 'Hong Qi'). Initial non-dominant syllables do not neutralise (asymmetry vs Zhong 2003, Lin 2011, Bao & Chen 2005). Caveat p. 17: targets were utterance-final, so phrasal stress overlaps lexical prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe urban Changsha Xiang (New Xiang, Changsha city, Hunan), 16 Changsha-raised native speakers; tone values after Zhong (2003). The glottocode's bundle name is 'Changsha dialect'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (world-2026-09-17) has an empty rule; the existing statement (Guo & Chen 2022) classes Changsha as a tone language with left-dominant (strong-weak) disyllabic prosodic words whose second syllable reduces to level tones. The SSRN abstract agrees on the tonal type and on final-syllable tonal neutralisation under initial stress, and adds (i) an explicit claim that this is word stress rather than tone sandhi, (ii) a second, final-stress word type, and (iii) a three-level stress scale with the initial syllable of final-stress words secondarily stressed. No contradiction in placement; it broadens 'left-dominant' to 'both initial- and final-stress words exist'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Changsha Xiang is a six-tone language in which the authors argue word stress coexists with lexical tone: disyllabic words come in an initial-stress type and a final-stress type (structure-dependent, per the same authors' slides after Lin 2011); in initial-stress words the final syllable is unstressed and its six tones neutralise to four short level tones, while in final-stress words the initial syllable is not unstressed but secondarily stressed and keeps its full tonal targets. The 'tone sandhi' of earlier descriptions is reinterpreted as this tone-stress interaction. No single fixed stress position is claimed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three stress levels posited (primary, secondary, none): the initial syllable of final-stress (right-dominant) disyllables is analysed as secondarily stressed, retaining underlying tonal targets, in contrast to the genuinely unstressed final syllable of initial-stress words, where tones merge into four level tones.
new_statements.exceptions: None visible in the abstract; which lexical/grammatical classes take final stress is not stated there (the authors' 2026 Lancaster slides, already held by the project, assign right-dominance to subject-predicate, verb-result, verb-object compounds and person/place names, left-dominance to coordinative and modifier-head compounds).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the Changsha city variety of Xiang (New Xiang), speakers raised in Changsha; the SSRN preprint is the submitted manuscript that became Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026, Journal of Phonetics 114:101472 (retitled 'Tone sandhi and tonal coarticulation in disyllabic sequences in Changsha Xiang').

tone_statements.quote: 房青（2009）的声学实验研究表明，湘潭方言共有五个单字调：阴平 33、阳平 12、上声 42、阴去 45、阳去 21。其中，原入声调已并入阳平调类。本文主要依据其调查材料，对湘潭方言两字组连读变调现象进行讨论。... 依据 Bao（1999）的声调表征模型，湘潭方言五个单字调可表征为：阴平[H, l]、阳平[L, lh]、上声[H, hl]、阴去[H, lh]、阳去[L, hl] ... 本文认为，湘潭方言的载调单位应为莫拉。其依据主要有两点：第一，湘潭方言存在轻声现象。... 第二，湘潭方言存在曲折调。
tone_statements.translation: Fang Qing's (2009) acoustic study shows that the Xiangtan dialect has five citation tones: yinping 33, yangping 12, shangsheng 42, yinqu 45, yangqu 21. The former entering tone has merged into the yangping category. This paper relies mainly on that study's survey materials to discuss disyllabic tone sandhi in Xiangtan ... Following Bao's (1999) tone-representation model the five citation tones can be represented as yinping [H, l], yangping [L, lh], shangsheng [H, hl], yinqu [H, lh], yangqu [L, hl] ... We hold that the tone-bearing unit of Xiangtan should be the mora, for two main reasons: first, Xiangtan has neutral tone ... second, Xiangtan has contour tones.
tone_statements.locator: p. 186 §1; feature representations and TBU sentence p. 187 §3
tone_statements.summary: Xiangtan Xiang: 5 citation tones (33 12 42 45 21, after Fang 2009), Bao register+contour features, TBU = mora; sandhi 'first changes, second keeps'; weak 2nd syllable of neutral-tone words loses tone.

tone_statements.translation: The Yiyang dialect has 5 citation tones (not counting the neutral tone): T1 yinping 33 ..., T2 yangping 13 ..., T3 shangsheng 41 ..., T4 qusheng 11 ..., T5 rusheng 45 ... By pitch value, yinping is mid level, yangping low rising, shangsheng falling, qusheng low level, rusheng high rising. When the level tones (yinping, qusheng) are in unstressed position their value does not change; when the non-level tones (yangping, shangsheng, rusheng) are unstressed they generally change, whatever the neighbouring tone, from rising or falling to level: yangping 13 > 33, shangsheng 41 > 11, rusheng 45 > 44.
tone_statements.summary: 5 citation tones; sandhi only in unstressed syllable (13>33, 41>11, 45>44). English abstract gives yinping 34, qusheng 21, but body has 33, 11. Sandhi domain = syllable (citing Lu 2006).

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources. Guo & Chen 2022 (catalog's existing statement) present Changsha as the representative left-dominant (initial-strong) dialect with right dominance confined to a few grammatical categories; Zhang, Gong & Guo 2026 (abstract plus their Lancaster slides) treat Changsha as having two coexisting, structure-dependent patterns (left-in the dominant set coordinative/modifier-head common nouns, right-in the dominant set subject-predicate, verb-result, verb-object and in all proper names) and stress the asymmetry of the reduction. That is a difference of emphasis and scope, not of placement. The only tension is on the label: Zhang et al. say only that the sandhi 'may reflect metrical prominence at the word level' and that more work is needed 'to establish stress in Changsha Xiang', whereas Guo & Chen speak of metrical structure/stress directly. The SSRN 2024 preprint could not be opened, so its position is unknown.

sources.access_detail: digital copy exists; only the abstract or an excerpt is open
sources.quote: [SSRN abstract, v2 4702575] Two experiments were conducted to investigate disyllabic words with initial and final stress. The F0 contour and duration analyses showed that the variability in tonal production could be grasped by the interaction of lexical tones and three different levels of stress: primary stress, secondary stress, and no stress. The so-called word-initial unstressed syllables are likelier to be “secondarily stressed” rather than “unstressed”. The six tones retained their underlying targets in both the primary-stressed and secondary-stressed syllables. In the word-final unstressed syllables, the tones merged into four level tones.
sources.locator: SSRN abstract page (v2 4702575, archived copy (Internet Archive, 11 Jun 2024); v1 4377641, capture 20250506151247), copies we hold
sources.note: The only work devoted specifically to word stress in Changsha Xiang (duration/F0 correlates, tone-stress interaction); would supersede Guo & Chen's cross-dialect statement.

tone.translation: Fang Qing's (2009) acoustic study shows that the Xiangtan dialect has five citation tones: yinping 33, yangping 12, shangsheng 42, yinqu 45, yangqu 21. The former entering tone has merged into the yangping category. This paper relies mainly on that study's survey materials to discuss disyllabic tone sandhi in Xiangtan ... tone.translation: The Yiyang dialect has 5 citation tones (not counting the neutral tone): T1 yinping 33 ..., T2 yangping 13 ..., T3 shangsheng 41 ..., T4 qusheng 11 ..., T5 rusheng 45 ... By pitch value, yinping is mid level, yangping low rising, shangsheng falling, qusheng low level, rusheng high rising. When the level tones (yinping, qusheng) are in unstressed position their value does not change; when the non-level tones (yangping, shangsheng, rusheng) are unstressed they generally change, whatever the neighbouring tone, from rising or falling to level: yangping 13 > 33, shangsheng 41 > 11, rusheng 45 > 44.
